Budget axe of small grant fund will hurt conservation groups across Australia | Environment

Between the papers of any federal budget are the places where ideologies are most strikingly revealed and alliances are displayed.

It's also a good place to drop a sounding line to fathom the true depth of a government’s collective likes and dislikes.

And so Prime Minister Tony Abbott’s first budget brought its weight to bear on climate change, renewable energy and the environment.

The wreckage has been well surveyed but one cut in particular shows how far the budget went to undermine Australia's conservation movement.

We know the big loser was renewable energy – the material scrapping of the $1.3 billion Australian Renewable Energy Agency and the disappearance of the “One Million Solar Roofs” pledge tells that story.

The CSIRO, the government’s science agency, says cuts to its budget will see as many as 500 people out of work.

About $20 million gets saved from merging key programs funding environment and climate change research. The Bureau of Meteorology loses $10 million over the next four years.

The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority now has $600,000 per year less at a time when the coastline is the focus of multiple new developments and facing an embarrassing “in danger” listing by the World Heritage Committee.

Not touched were subsidies to fossil fuel companies and miners, such as the tax credit that saves multi-billion dollar firms about $2.4 billion a year on their fuel costs.

But arguably the most revealing of all the cuts was the axing of a small $1.3 million program that has been a key resource of local and state-based conservation groups across Australia for 40 years.

Established in 1973, the Grants to Voluntary Environment, Sustainability and Heritage Organisations had been supporting more than a 150 groups across the country.

Conservation groups have told me the cut will be felt across Australia, with some smaller groups facing the threat of closure.

In effect, the cut undermines the effectiveness of grassroots, community-based conservation groups to engage with people where they live and to work with local councils and state governments.

Many of the grants are tiny - $2,000 here and $3,000 there - but critically, its larger grants of up to $77,000 have gone to state-based environment groups that act as support bodies for a multitude of smaller local volunteer-run groups.

Cutting the fund is like pulling out a keystone that holds Australia’s community-run conservation movement together.The fund helped groups to run events, write submissions, attend meetings, engage in public consultation and keep the lights on.

Charlie Sherwin is chief executive of Environment Tasmania that got $50,000 annually from the fund in recent years. The annual grant represented more than 10 per cent of the group’s annual income.

He told me:

> This cut hurts us. It matters to us. These grants have been supported by governments of all flavours for a long time. They give core administrative funding to small community organisations that in turn give support to other community organisations. It’s an insult to a lot of people who work really hard for nothing.
> 
> We have a lot of members who work flat out, week after week, looking after the land and sea and they expect to get only a tiny token of respect from their federal government and that has been taken away. It’s an act of disrespect.

Mark Wakeham, acting CEO at Environment Victoria that has been getting $77,000 a year from the fund, says:

> It was contributing to the cost of keeping the doors open for a lot of groups – everything from covering public liability insurance at events to providing a photocopier when groups want to hand out information.

Wakeham says there was no warning about the cut and he said Environment Victoria had spoken with Environment Minister Greg Hunt who had said he would try and continue the programme. Evidently, Hunt failed. Wakeham added:


> It’s deeply disappointing and will affect volunteer-run conservation groups across the country. Community groups need some infrastructure and support. That infrastructure is now being cut adrift.

Peter McGlone, the director of the Tasmanian Conservation Trust, said his group had been working hard on issues like invasive species and fisheries management. Unless the funds could be made up, he said the loss of the annual $40,000 from the fund could see them lose one of their three staff members. He said:


> This cut pushes us away from being able to contribute in an informed way. Frankly, it’s ideological. The government is telling the broader Australian community that it does not want to sit down in a civil way and hear what conservation groups have to say on government policies.

Toby Hutcheon, executive director at the Queensland Conservation Council, said the cuts were “disastrous”. QCC’s annual grant of $77,000 represented about a third of his organisation’s income.


Other groups affected include Keep Australia Beautiful, the Nature Conservation Council of NSW, the Australian Marine Conservation Society, the Alternative Technology Association and the main conservation councils of WA, South Australia, ACT and more than 100 other smaller groups.

Victoria McKenzie-McHarg is the climate change manager at the Australian Conservation Foundation that’s not directly impacted by the cuts. But I’ll leave you with her thoughts.

> This will have a dire impact. It’s starting to look like [the Government] are trying to silence environmental organisations.
> 
> Most of these organisations operate on the smell of an oily rag. This program has been their bread and butter and has allowed them to keep the doors open and provide a community voice for the environment around the country.
> 
> When faced with a so-called budget emergency, it is remarkable to see $1.3 million cut from environment groups while handing out $13 billion over the next few years to subsidise big polluting industries.

webpage.text:
I am and I am not Aboriginal | Jared Field

> Do I contradict myself?
> Very well then I contradict myself,
> (I am large, I contain multitudes.)
> 
> Walt Whitman,
> 51, Song of Myself, Leaves of Grass

I wonder how it felt, the first time she called herself Aboriginal. Was the pain sharp and surprising like glass in the foot? Or was it dull, soft, slow – expected even? On the banks of the Mehi river my grandmother was not born Aboriginal, she was born Kamilaroi. She became Aboriginal only much later.

My mother, however, was born Aboriginal and of that she is proud. In a way, this label forced on her mother had worked its colonial-magic. But to other Aboriginal people, she will always say she is Kamilaroi, from up Moree way, from Gomeroi clan. Her roots, too deep to really touch, run all the way to the Mehi.

With me, and many others of my age, this colonial-magic has had more time to soak in. It is now in the red soil in which we grew. I was born Aboriginal.

For us now the question is mostly: but how much?

My lighter-skinned cousins, in one ugly volte-face, are being stripped of this label. All the while, my honey-coloured skin and hazel-coloured eyes betray me. Which is to say, I’m allowed the label but must add the fine print: half-half dilution (little do they know that I am in fact double). My darker-skinned cousins, however, are marked by their glorious shade; like it or not, the label is theirs.

In a way, my generation is like dried fruit. Most of the substance – Gomeroi clan, Kamilaroi nation – was sucked out. Instead of something ripe we are left mostly with dried skin, labels and bits of flesh – from up Moree way – raisins and sultanas that are told they are not grapes.

But this isn’t all bad. Dried fruit is made to last.

The Palyku nation in the far west has a culture entirely distinct to the Kamilaroi nation in the east. The lands we are custodians of are different, our gods are different, our languages are different. Nyiyaparli to Kamilaroi is like French to Russian. What then did our born-again Aboriginal grandmothers really have in common? An oppressor.

Let that soak in.

So now, as Naidoc week approaches, I ask: what good is this label?

On the one hand, between Aboriginal people, it builds connection and breeds camaraderie. Here in Oxford, miles from home, it has allowed me to spin friendships into the stuff of families. It is a secret though sometimes unrecognised nod to the unspoken: those doing me wrong are the very same doing wrong to you. Repurposed, used with ourselves and among ourselves, this label can be an act of rebellion.

For this reason, to fellow Indigenous people, I will always be Aboriginal.

On the other, it ensures the continuation of a word often used to denigrate my grandmother, my mother and myself. It, and its repulsive diminutive, were uttered when children were taken. They were uttered when my mother as a child was chased out of the cinema with a metal bar. They were uttered on my first day of university. Perhaps worse still, it still erases our rich and beautiful diversity. In short, it fulfills its original function.

For this reason, to non-Indigenous people, I will never again be Aboriginal.

Instead, now tasting the Mehi, I am Gomeroi from the Kamilaroi nation. To say so is to perform real magic. Bit by bit the original labelling is dissolved like aspirin in water. Word by word sovereignty is exerted.

I am and I am not Aboriginal. The fruit was dried but the seed was not.

> I concentrate toward them that are nigh, I wait on the door-slab.
> Who has done his day’s work? who will soonest be through with his supper?
> Who wishes to walk with me?
> 
> Walt Whitman,
> 51, Song of Myself, Leaves of Grass

Climate change: farmers urge Coalition to restore emissions trading scheme | Emissions trading

A delegation of farmers has called for the Abbott government to act on climate change by restoring an emissions trading scheme, maintaining the current renewable energy target and spending on rail infrastructure to improve inland transport and reduce carbon emissions.

The farmers have spent two days lobbying the Coalition to start implementing a suite of policies to deal with the effects of climate change, warning of dire consequences for the agriculture sector if the threat was not addressed.

They have told the government MPs, including John Cobb and the staff of the treasurer Joe Hockey, that the Direct Action policy, which provides incentives for polluters to reduce carbon emissions, will not work to ameliorate climate change, “but if the government wants to give away money, people will keep taking it”.

The delegation said the lack of climate policies was being exacerbated by the cuts to research and development funding for applied climate science and the Bureau of Meteorology.

The visit came as intense negotiations between the government and Labor continued over the RET, which currently requires the government to source 41,000 gigawatt hours of energy from renewables by 2020. The latest government offer to Labor is 32,000GWh.

It also follows a report by University of Melbourne researchers called Appetite for Change, which charted the detrimental effects of climate change on Australia’s food production.

The farmers, organised by Earth Hour Australia, said the Abbott government needed to show leadership on the issue and it could start by using the term climate change, rather than “climate variability”.

John Pettigrew, who has an irrigation property at Bunbartha north of Shepperton, said calling climate change “variability” was “doing everyone a disservice”.

“We are not going to revert to where we were 10 years ago,” said Pettigrew. “There will be highs and lows, but the trend is there. We saw it through the millennium drought and failing to acknowledge the problem is only adding to it.

“It’s doing the industry a disservice. It’s about how the industry is perceived by overseas buyers. Already in dairy, large multinational companies are demanding environment and carbon emission recording to show it’s been factored in.

“The Australian government’s international perception is not good [on climate change] and that is an impediment to us being able to get into high-value markets.”

Peter Holding, who runs a 1500-hectare farm at Harden west of Canberra, said the science indicated that climate change was a bigger issue than the weather and Australia needed to protect its international reputation.

“We want to see some leadership, we are tired of platitudes and saying it can’t happen, we are losing markets because Australia’s reputation is slipping on being clean and green,” Holding said.

“Climate change going to have impacts right across the budget from dislocation of whole rural communities to drought assistance.

“We need infrastructure spending and new industries in the renewable energy sector. Governments have to start thinking on policies that last a bit longer than a three year term.”

Holding said while some carbon farming initiatives such as methane capture in piggeries were effective, Direct Action was generally rolling out slowly and farmers and researchers remain unconvinced the policy will meet any targets.

“People will be more than willing to accept the funding but we – and the research – are not convinced you can make a difference to climate change by doing it and therefore it is a waste of precious government funds, but if the government wants to give away money, people will keep taking it” said Holding.

Sid Plant, a grazier on the Darling Downs in Queensland, would like to see an emissions trading scheme, like the one first negotiated in 2009 by Kevin Rudd, Malcolm Turnbull and Ian Macfarlane.

Plant said he was hopeful that “something sensible” on emissions trading was proposed because he believes it would allow farmers to benefit from increasing organic carbon in the soil, which had added benefits for the farm as well as turning a profit.

“I hoped to position myself to have carbon to sell and it might not pay a lot but there will be benefits for increasing organic carbon, such as retaining more moisture,” he said.

Plant’s family has farmed for seven generations and he first had to study weather patterns to get his pilot’s licence. He first noticed the El Nino pattern in 1973 and learned to apply the science to better manage his cattle. Under a changing climate, Plant no longer keeps a breeding herd so that he can sell down as soon as the weather turns dry. He is convinced he will not see much rain from now until Christmas.

“The most significant part of climate change is declining rainfall, which applies to most of Queensland,” Plant said.

“Australian farmers are feeling climate change as early as anybody in the world, and significantly, we have the world’s highest year to year rainfall variability.

“Climate change is coming over the top and when the UN sees our farmers as leading the world, we seem to be running out of bright ideas without the right policies. I want to save world for my grandchildren.

“I find it very difficult to find someone to vote for.”
